judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: A 30x30 image (a blue swirl logo with no text) is the only content of a footer link to https://itargettecnologia.com.br (the site developer, iTarget Tecnologia), alt and title 'itarget-icon'; the live HTML is the same. Applying R2's first test, the alternative read as the link's text names iTarget, the company whose site the link opens, so it lets users tell where the link goes; it is clumsy and file-name-like ('-icon'), but it does not lose the destination (compare an alt such as 'facebook-icon' on a Facebook link). The claim's second half, that it does not say where the link leads, is therefore not true, and the element meets 1.1.1 on this point (a better alt would be 'iTarget Tecnologia'). The icon lies just below the full screenshot's bottom edge, but the crop and the live page agree with the snapshot.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: Footer image under the h5 'Fliliada a:' (affiliated to): the logo of AMB with the words 'AMB Associação Médica Brasileira', not a link, alt and title 'csm_logo_amb2' (a CMS file name), the same on the live page. As an auditor I would fail it under 1.1.1 (F30, file name as text alternative; it leaves out the organisation's name that the image shows and wraps the acronym in 'csm_' and '2'). But competent auditors would disagree both on whether an alt that still contains 'amb' fails, and on whether 'describes something the image does not show' names a file-name defect, so the label is uncertain.
